what_it_does: Large language models store billions of numerical weights. To reduce storage and speed up inference, a common technique is to round those weights down to lower-precision integers (for example, storing each weight in 4 bits instead of 16), while keeping the live activations — the intermediate values produced as data flows through the model — at full floating-point precision. The mismatch creates a practical problem: before a GPU can multiply a low-precision integer weight against a full-precision floating-point activation, it must first unpack and convert the integer back to floating-point, which largely erases the efficiency gain. PacQ proposes a microarchitecture — the internal design of a GPU-like processor — that sidesteps this conversion by building a new type of multiplier unit that can directly multiply an integer weight against a floating-point activation without the intermediate conversion step. The design also rethinks how data is packed and fed to these units so that many weights can be processed simultaneously, aiming to make weight-only quantization genuinely faster in hardware rather than just smaller on disk.
